--- title: "Specification curve" subtitle: "The curve of the claim" execute: echo: false warning: false message: false bibliography: [references.bib, references-new.bib] --- The specification curve presented on this page brings together every specification retained by the [specification menu](menu.qmd) for the claim examined in the Housing and racial bias case study, 64 in all, each fitted on the 1,014 emails of the Housing data. The claim, in the wording taken by SCORE from the paper by the original authors [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect], is that "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts". A specification, as the term is used here, is one complete set of answers to the decisions of an analysis. Five decisions vary on the curve: the comparison group (white names, or white and Black names together), the emails counted (the replies, or every delivered email), the replies without a greeting code (left out, or counted as no greeting), the model (a difference in proportions, or a logistic regression) and the adjustment (none, or one of three sets of covariates), which yields 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 4 = 64 specifications. Every specification leaves out the bounced emails, pools the male and the female names, counts every reply whoever wrote it, is tested by its own model and reports the gap in percentage points, while the [decision map](menu.qmd#map) presents every decision, including the options that are not on the curve, with the reason for each. ```{=html}
Specification curve of the claim
64 specifications, with the published result, the five reanalyses and the replication
Each mark is one specification: a circle for p < 0.05 and a cross for p ≥ 0.05 under the test of its own model. All 64 specifications are circles. The tags mark the published result of the original authors (OAs 2017), the five analysts of the robustness study and the replication in the SCORE replicability study (SCORE 2020), each placed by its gap in percentage points; the replication comes from new data. Click or tap a tag to hold its details open, and click again to release it. Colour by colours the marks by one decision and adds rows under the curve that show where the specifications using each option fall in the ranking; Show only keeps the specifications that use one option and fades the rest. Hover over or tap a mark for its details, or focus the chart and use the arrow keys.
Data: data/spec_curve.csv and data/reference_marks.csv, with their codebooks.
``` All 64 specifications lie below zero, in the direction of the claim, with estimates ranging from −20.0 to −12.1 points, and since all 64 have p < 0.05 under the test of their own model, every mark on the chart is a circle and the shaded band above zero remains empty. The reference specification compares Hispanic with white names among the replies, with a difference in proportions and no covariates, and reproduces the raw gap in the paper: 41.2% of the replies to Hispanic names opened with the name of the sender, against 61.1% of the replies to white names, a gap of −19.97 points. This specification lies at the left end of the curve, level with the logistic regression without covariates, which reproduces the same two shares. ## Reading the curve {#reading} Each mark represents one specification, the marks being ranked by their estimate from the largest gap on the left to the smallest on the right. The estimate is the difference in the share of greetings by name between Hispanic names and the comparison names, expressed in percentage points, the scale on which the abstract of the paper states the finding ("twenty percentage points"). While a linear probability model yields that difference as its coefficient, a logistic regression yields it as an average marginal effect, that is, the difference in the predicted probability of a named greeting between a Hispanic and a comparison name, averaged over the analysed emails, which places the two models on one scale. A value below zero means that Hispanic names were greeted by name less often, the direction of the claim, while the shaded band above zero would contain the results running against the claim. The shape of a mark indicates its class at the 5% level, an open circle standing for p < 0.05 and a cross for p ≥ 0.05. The p-value comes from the two-sided test of the model of each specification, a t with HC2 standard errors for the linear model and a Wald z for the logistic regression, which is the test that a single analyst would report. On this curve the p-values range from 0.00001 to 0.0010, which means that every specification clears the threshold by a wide margin, that the shape carries no information and that what varies between the specifications is the size of the gap. The pop-up of each mark also reports the p-value of a randomisation test, which reshuffles the names among the analysed emails 1,999 times and refits the model after each reshuffle, a p-value that is at most 0.0030 across the curve. Every test on the curve is two-sided, whereas a one-tailed test halves the p-value by fixing the direction of the gap in advance, a choice that the menu treats as a weaker answer and that the paper makes only for the gap in replies, as the section [beside the curve](#beside) shows. Under *Colour by*, an option that pushes results towards one end of the curve appears as a bunched row of ticks, and colouring by the emails counted divides the curve into two blocks, while *Show only* reports how many specifications are shown and how many of these lie below zero with p < 0.05. The pop-up of a mark gives the full recipe of the specification, the number of emails analysed and the two shares behind the gap, and the button above the chart downloads the data from which the chart is drawn, with the option codes taken as arguments by `try_spec()`. The share of specifications that agree with the claim describes this set of analyses and should not be read as the probability that the claim is true, a distinction explained in [section 6 of the multiverse module](companion/multiverse.qmd#sec-reading). ## Reference marks {#reference-marks} Seven tagged marks come from outside the curve: the published result of the original authors, tagged OAs 2017, the five reanalyses of the claim recorded in the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], tagged by the identifiers of the analysts, and the replication of the paper in the SCORE replicability study, tagged SCORE 2020. As the replication comes from new data, its mark, at zero, stands apart from the curve, and the way in which the course computed this mark is explained on the [background page](background.qmd#replication-scale). Every mark is placed by its gap in percentage points, the published result by the number that the paper gives on that scale, the change in the predicted probability of a named greeting from a white to a Hispanic name with the other variables at their means, −20.0 points with a 95% confidence interval from −30.5 to −10.0 (p. 18 of the accepted manuscript). The five analyses are placed by the course refits of the analysts' scripts on the public file, refits that reproduce exactly the four statistics recorded in the robustness study and that place P9W8Y, for whom the robustness study recorded no statistic, by the model in the analyst's report. ::: {#tbl-marks .cell tbl-cap='The six reference marks of the original data: the statistic as published or recorded, the emails analysed, the gap in percentage points by which the mark is placed, the number of specifications on the curve that lie further below zero, and where the result stands in relation to the menu. Sources: `data/reference_marks.csv`, `data/analysts5.csv`.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Mark Statistic Emails Gap (points) Further below zero Relation to the menu
OAs 2017 z = −3.73 549 −20.0 0 outside the menu
UYV3F z = −3.771 362 −20.0 0 on the curve
P9W8Y χ2(2) = 15.951 (refit) 558 −20.0 0 beside the curve (three-group model)
EWFMI z = 3.645 549 −19.4 8 outside the menu
8PTRZ χ2 = 14.265 558 −17.3 16 on the curve
25N5D χ2 = 13.683 665 −13.2 36 on the curve
``` ::: ::: Three of the analyses correspond to points on the curve itself. 8PTRZ compared Hispanic names with white and Black names together among the replies, UYV3F fitted a logistic regression without covariates to the replies to Hispanic and white names, and 25N5D counted every delivered email, with the uncoded replies treated as no greeting. In each case the gap obtained by the refit equals the gap of the matching specification, and the test reported by the analyst – the $\chi^2$ test of a table, a z or a two-proportion test – serves as a check of the test that classes the point. P9W8Y fitted the three groups in one model without covariates, a model that yields exactly the raw gap of the reference specification, and then reported whether the three groups differ at all. EWFMI and the original authors, by contrast, fitted models outside the menu, EWFMI adjusting, beside the hard-to-find address, for the sex of the name and for the poverty third entered as a number, and the original authors for the continuous census values replaced with thirds in the public file. Refitted on these thirds, the original authors' model yields −18.4 points (z = −3.47), which is why the mark retains the published number and the refit is not drawn. The mark of 25N5D lies among the specifications that count every delivered email, while the other five marks lie among the specifications that count the replies. Two of the six results, those of 25N5D and P9W8Y, come from analysts who concluded in Task 1 of the robustness study that the data showed no evidence either way, although both marks are circles, and how each verdict came about is explained on the [background page](background.qmd#sec-verdicts). ## What moved the estimate {#shifts} Every option on the curve can be compared with the first option of its decision on twin specifications, which agree on every other decision, and @fig-shifts summarises the effect of each option on the estimate. Counting every delivered email instead of the replies moves the estimate by +4.95 points on average, towards zero (from +3.66 to +6.70 across its 32 pairs), from a mean of −17.7 points among the replies to −12.7 among all delivered emails, whereas no other option moves any specification by more than 2.7 points. Pooling the Black names with the white ones moves the estimate by +1.27 points on average, the adjustment for the size and poverty of the community by +0.95 and the set that also includes its ethnic composition by +1.06, while counting the uncoded replies as no greeting moves it by +0.34, adjusting for the hard-to-find address by +0.08 and fitting a logistic regression by −0.01. Part of the shift under the two community sets is attributable to the 14 emails left out by these sets for want of community thirds. No option moves any specification across the 5% threshold. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![What each option on the curve does to the estimate, against the first option of its decision on twin specifications: the mean shift (point) and the smallest and largest shift (line), in percentage points. A positive shift moves the estimate towards zero. Source: `data/menu_deviations.csv`.](curve_files/figure-html/fig-shifts-1.png){#fig-shifts fig-alt='Dot-and-range chart of seven options. All delivered emails shifts the estimate by about +5 points, from about +3.7 to +6.7; the other six options lie between about −0.1 and +2.7 points, most of them near zero.' width=720} ::: ::: Split by decision, the variance of the 64 estimates is almost entirely attributable to the emails counted, which explain 86.7% of it, against 5.7% for the comparison group, 3.3% for the adjustment, 0.4% for the uncoded replies, 0.0% for the model, and 3.9% for the interactions between decisions. Among the replies, the estimates range from −20.0 to −15.8 points, and among all delivered emails from −13.3 to −12.1. The decision on the emails counted moves the estimate most, since it changes the outcome as well as the rows. Only 53% to 61% of the delivered emails in each group drew a reply, and since among all delivered emails an email without a reply counts as one without a named greeting, the shares of named greetings there are roughly half the shares among the replies, with the gap between the groups shrinking accordingly. Counting every delivered email preserves the groups as randomisation made them, whereas the comparison among replies is a pure effect of the name only if the name did not change which officials replied, the post-treatment problem raised by analyst 25N5D and discussed on the [background page](background.qmd#sec-posttreatment) and in the [causal-graphs module](companion/dags.qmd#sec-case). The curve retains both comparisons as two estimands, and its two blocks are thus answers to two related questions, with the consequence that the spread between the two blocks does not represent uncertainty about one quantity. ## Beside the curve {#beside} Several findings of the paper remain off the curve, since each answers a question other than the claim, and the three displays below present these findings. ### Other outcomes and the Black names {#outcomes} The paper also asks whether officials replied at all and whether they replied within 24 hours, and it compares the Black names with the white ones on every outcome, comparisons presented beside the greeting in @tbl-outcomes. ::: {#tbl-outcomes .cell tbl-cap='Four outcomes, for the Hispanic and the Black names against the white names: the difference in percentage points, as a difference in proportions with an HC2 test, two-sided. Source: `data/display_outcomes.csv`.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Outcome Hispanic names Emails Black names Emails
Any reply, among delivered emails −4.8 (p = 0.214) 665 3.3 (p = 0.404) 634
Reply within 24 hours, among replies 2.1 (p = 0.642) 364 4.5 (p = 0.297) 372
Greeted by name, among coded replies −20.0 (p = 0.0001) 362 −5.0 (p = 0.328) 371
Greeted by name, among delivered emails −13.3 (p = 0.0001) 662 −1.0 (p = 0.789) 630
``` ::: ::: Emails with Hispanic names drew a reply 4.8 points less often than emails with white names, with p = 0.214 two-sided, a gap for which the paper reports p = .11 and which it calls "borderline significant (with a one-tailed test)" (p. 15), while the one-tailed p of the same test is 0.107. As a one-tailed test is defensible only when the direction was fixed before anyone looked at the data, the curve retains two-sided tests throughout. Replies to Hispanic names came within 24 hours 2.1 points more often than replies to white names (p = 0.642). No comparison comes near significance for the Black names, which drew a reply 3.3 points more often than the white names and whose replies opened with the name 5.0 points less often (p = 0.328). These differences correspond to other claims of the same paper, concerning access rather than tone or another group, and they remain off the curve. ### Subgroups {#subgroups} While the curve pools the male and the female names and counts every reply, whoever wrote it, @fig-subgroups splits the reference comparison in three ways: by the sex of the name, by whether the official who replied had a Hispanic name, and by the third of the community on percent Hispanic. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The gap in greetings by name between Hispanic and white names among the coded replies, in subgroups, with 95% confidence intervals from HC2 standard errors. Circles have p < 0.05 and crosses p ≥ 0.05; the burgundy row is the reference comparison. Source: `data/display_subgroups.csv`.](curve_files/figure-html/fig-subgroups-1.png){#fig-subgroups fig-alt='Dot-and-interval chart of eight rows. All names −20.0; male names −23.3, female names −15.7; officials with Hispanic names −25.7 with a very wide interval crossing zero; other officials −19.8; lower, middle and top thirds of percent Hispanic −20.7, −14.8 and −22.5, the middle third crossing zero.' width=720} ::: ::: The gap is −23.3 points between Santiago and Brett (p = 0.0009, 201 replies) and −15.7 points between Gabriela and Emily (p = 0.046, 161 replies). Each half answers a narrower question, about men or about women, and the replication used male names only. Among the 28 replies from officials with Hispanic names the gap is −25.7 points (p = 0.184), against −19.8 among the 334 replies from other officials, but this subgroup is selected after the email arrived, since an official is known only by replying, and it is also small. By the Hispanic third of the community, the gap is −20.7 points in the lower third, −14.8 in the middle third and −22.5 in the top third, a pattern that cannot be distinguished from a single gap, given the width of the intervals. The [audit-experiments module](companion/experiments.qmd#sec-names) examines what the names convey and explains why a subgroup of officials is a different kind of split from a subgroup of names. ### The randomisation distribution {#randomisation} Since the names were assigned to the housing authorities at random, the gap that chance alone produces can be found by reshuffling the names. For @fig-ri, the names were reshuffled among the 362 coded replies to Hispanic and white names 4,999 times, and the gap was recomputed after each reshuffle. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The gap in greetings by name between Hispanic and white names among the coded replies, after each of 4,999 random reshuffles of the names among those replies. The dashed lines enclose the central 95% of the reshuffled gaps, and the burgundy line marks the observed gap. Source: `data/display_ri.csv`.](curve_files/figure-html/fig-ri-1.png){#fig-ri fig-alt='Histogram of reshuffled gaps centred on zero, mostly between about −10 and +10 points, with a burgundy line at the observed gap of about −20 points, in the far left tail.' width=720} ::: ::: The central 95% of the reshuffled gaps lies between −10.0 and +9.9 points, and a gap at least as large in absolute value as the observed −19.97 occurs in 1 of the 4,999 reshuffles. Requiring no model of the errors, only the fact that the names were assigned at random, the test agrees with the test of the model, which suggests that within the original data chance is a poor explanation of the gap.
